text: Abstract The continuous growth of patent literature has placed new demands on technological innovation and automated processing, particularly in the task of extracting Subject-Action-Object (SAO) relationships. This study constructs an information extraction benchmark framework tailored for the collaborative robotics domain, comparing three large language models—GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet—and their corresponding agents. The experimental design employs a closed-loop “reflection and refinement” model, integrating the thought chain and ReAct method strategies, and configures decoding parameters to prioritize factual quality over linguistic diversity in extraction results. The experimental results indicate that the agent architecture has a positive impact on the performance of all models. Among them, the Gemini 1.5 Pro agent performed the best, achieving an F1 score of 89.58% (95% confidence interval: [87.9%, 91.2%]) and a BERTScore of 87.73%. A t-test statistical significance analysis based on 501 independent test sentence samples confirmed that the agent significantly outperforms baseline large language models, particularly in the parsing of recursively nested clauses and the filtering of legal jargon. Resource consumption analysis indicates that although the agent framework results in a 40- to 60-fold increase in computational cost—consuming an average of 11,000 to 15,000 tokens per sentence—this overhead is justified in specific patent analysis scenarios due to its superior recall performance and risk mitigation effects. Furthermore, by classifying typical failure modes and proposing a hierarchical deployment strategy, this study provides a methodological framework and empirical foundation for deploying and applying the agent in specific technical domains. Similar content being viewed by others Introduction Patents serve as a valuable asset to promote scientific innovation, they contain a lot of technical, economic, and legal information, which will significantly impact the progression of science and industry. Since the global technology competition has increased, the volume of patents have increased significantly. Due to this, traditional manual techniques for analyzing and extracting the core technical information from patents are difficult to use and/or limited in their ability to do so. Consequently, the need for the development of new and improved methods for processing patent information efficiently and accurately has arisen. The Subject-Action-Object (SAO) structure was introduced during this period of time to help create a more uniformed approach to analyzing patent information. The SAO model maps technical items along with the functional elements of technical items where the SAO model converts unstructured data into structured triples that will assist in the process of information extraction and the mapping of technology1,2. Therefore, researchers are using the SAO approaches to discover the core technology3, follow the path of innovation4, evaluate the similarity5 and provide the higher standard of the patent analysis. In the era of Industry 5.0, collaborative robots serve as a key vehicle for human-robot collaboration. Integrating technologies such as intelligent control and automated production, they are widely used in industries including manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare6,7,8,9, providing a data foundation and real-world scenarios for large-scale information extraction. However, this field spans multiple disciplines, including artificial intelligence, mechanical engineering, and software design, resulting in highly heterogeneous technical language and complex structures within patent texts—making it difficult for traditional information analysis methods to accurately analyze them. Consequently, SAO structure extraction can effectively parse these technical relationships and innovation, promoting the integration and development of cross-disciplinary technologies. Selecting the collaborative robotics field as the research subject allows for the full utilization of its abundant patent data resources, providing a scientific basis for the optimization and application of related technologies. In recent years, advancements in the field of artificial intelligence have spurred a surge of benchmarking research focused on evaluating the capabilities of large language models and intelligent agents10,11. However, benchmarks such as MMLU primarily focus on assessing models’ general reasoning abilities or their ability to use tools. In the field of information extraction, existing general-purpose evaluation schemes typically target simplified entity or relation extraction tasks, making it difficult to reflect a model’s ability to address the “syntactic fragility” unique to patents—patent texts are characterized by dense technical terminology, complex recursive syntactic structures, and formulaic legal language12,13. A significant research gap currently exists: there is no rigorous benchmarking scheme to evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art large language models and specialized agents when tackling such challenging tasks. To address this shortcoming, this study constructs a specialized information extraction benchmark using collaborative robot patents as corpus. We systematically evaluated the upper performance limits of large language models combined with agents when processing extreme syntactic complexity, thereby providing an empirical foundation for deploying agents in high-risk patent intelligence scenarios such as freedom-to-operate analysis. Against this backdrop, key questions that remain to be addressed include: how performance varies across different model architectures; what the practical trade-offs are between performance, cost, and latency; and what are the underlying mechanisms behind model failures.
